newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Ind prod data underlines fast Portugal GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Ind prod data underlines fast Portugal GDP growth.

text.p: A surge in the industrial production index in April raises prospects that Gross Domestic Product could grow by as much as 3.5 percent in Portugal this year, analysts said.
But they added that despite the quickening growth, inflationary tensions are not on the horizon and the Bank of Portugal still has room to cut key rates further.

Portugal's index of industrial production rose by 4.7 percent in April, compared with the same year-ago period, and by 0.3 percent compared with March, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE).
"This is a very good industrial production figure and allied to the latest jobs figures underlines an acceleration in economic growth," said Isabel Costa, analyst of Finantia.
Portugal's unemployment rate, announced last Friday, dropped to 6.5 percent in the second quarter from 7.3 percent in the first quarter and 7.2 percent in the second quarter of 1996.
Pedro Braz Teixeira, analyst of Banco Santander de Negocios Portugal, said conditions pointed to revising GDP growth forecasts for 1997 above 3.50 percent.

The Bank of Portugal forecast in a report in March that GDP growth would stand at between 3.0 and 3.75 percent in 1997, compared with an estimate of 3.3 percent in 1996, figures considered by some analysts at the time of publication of the report as exaggerated.
The latest industrial production and jobless data point to a strengthening in GDP growth, but analysts said they had not detected inflationary tensions.
"On the supply side, I don't see price pressures, and I don't see them on the demand side either because it is not certain that consumption is recovering," said Isabel Cabral of Lisbon broker Fincor.
Costa said: "Even considering the increase in the rate of capacity utilisation, the inflation picture is not worrying."
In the first quarter of 1997, the rate of productive capacity utilisation in the manufacturing industry stood at 80.3 percent, 2.9 percentage points more than in the first quarter of 1996.

In May the consumer prices index rose 0.7 percent, compared with 0.2 percent in April and 0.5 percent in May 1996. Prices rose by 2.1 percent year-on-year in May, compared with 1.8 percent in April and 3.5 percent in May 1996.
Portuguese Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco said that the disappointing May figure was an exceptional result, caused by sharp increases in food prices, that should not be repeated.
Braz Teixeira said: "Even if consumption recovers, I don't see much inflationary pressure in the coming months."

A London analyst said: "With inflation under control, the Bank of Portugal has to cut rates because the theory that the economy is growing well and so no more cuts are necessary conflicts with Portugal's need to meet convergence targets for the euro."
Costa said the differential between Spanish and Portuguese key rates was very high and was not justified by the economic fundamentals of the two countries.
The Portuguese repo rate is 6.0 percent and the draining rate is 5.70 percent, compared with a Spanish repo rate of 5.25 percent.
